title: Forecasting Demand Using Linear Regression

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the following statistical terms: regression coefficient, standard error, t-statistic, p-value, R-squared
Know how to run a regression model in Excel
Know and understand how to interpret and use regression output

keyTerms.def: The line that minimizes the sum of squared deviations between the line and the actual data points. Y = a + bX, where a and b are parameters that define the intercept and slope. Objective: estimate the parameters that define the true relationship between Y and X(s).

Estimates of the true parameters that define the relationship between dependent and independent variables. Interpretation: 'A one-unit increase in x leads to (magnitude of coefficient) increase/decrease (sign of coefficient) in y.'
The standard deviation of the parameter estimate; a measure of how noisy our estimate is. The smaller/greater the standard error, the more/less precise your parameter estimate.

The ratio of the parameter estimate (regression coefficient) to its standard error. Generally, t-statistics greater than 2 in absolute value indicate the coefficient is statistically significant (not equal to zero).

An alternative measure of statistical significance; per the slides, it 'tells you the probability that a true parameter that you estimated is equal to zero.' By convention, a coefficient is statistically significant when its p-value is less than 0.05.

Coefficient of determination; a measure of model fit equal to explained variation over total variation; ranges from 0 to 1. 'An R-squared of ___ indicates that ___% of the variation in y can be explained by variation in the x's.'
R-squared penalized for the number of variables the model uses.
Multiple regression isolates the effect of one variable holding others constant (the airline fare example; Netflix growth and season removed).

workedExamples.name: Redstone Residential
workedExamples.givens: 10 complexes; Q on rent, advertising ($100s), distance (miles)
workedExamples.answer: Q = 135.15 − 0.14P + 0.54A − 5.78D; R² 0.79; adj 0.69; F 7.59 (p 0.018); distance significant (p 0.004); price borderline (t −2.41, p 0.053); advertising not (p 0.43); $100 rent increase → −14.3 units; OPE at means = −0.143 × 420/53.1 = −1.13 → elastic → raising rent lowers revenue

workedExamples.name: Airline cost per mile (CQ5)
workedExamples.answer: +100k passengers → −0.027¢/mile; 72.2% explained; departures significant; 200 extra miles → 1.4¢ difference; +17,000 departures → +0.88¢

workedExamples.name: Netflix subscription regression
workedExamples.answer: Price coefficient: ~596K fewer subscribers per $1 (t −2.97, p 0.013); OPE at $10 in 2011-Q2 ≈ −0.25; revenue-max price ≈ $25.25

cases: Airline Industry Revisited: Cincinnati 0.22 $/mile rank 1; Atlanta 0.20; SLC 0.17; Boston 0.14; LA 0.12 — how do you isolate the effect of individual variables? (S09 slides p.9; S01 slides pp.60-67)
WSJ 'The Most Expensive Airports to Fly To' (May 22, 2014): wealthy communities and business travelers → higher fares; busy airports → lower fares (S09 slides pp.7-8)

Netflix Revisited: raw data −855K per $1; growth and season removed −596K per $1; waterfall 9.3M + 13.9M growth + 3.7M season − 3.6M price (6 × 596K) = 23.4M predicted vs 21.7M actual 2011-Q4 (S09 slides pp.10-14)
Demand curves are dynamic: Redbox 2011 vs 2014 (S09 slides p.4)
Same cost, different margin: Netflix vs Redbox 2016-2 gross margin ~41% vs ~30%, operating expenses ~7% vs ~6% (S09 slides p.5)
traps: Check the UNITS of each x (passengers in 100,000s, departures in 1,000s, advertising in $100s)
Significance: |t| > 2 OR p < 0.05 — look at the right row
R² vs adjusted R² vs Multiple R
Small samples: |t| > 2 rule can disagree with p < 0.05 (Redstone price t = −2.41, p = 0.053)
When forecasting, plug in ALL variables (including dummies) for the scenario
Elasticity from a linear regression requires a P and Q at which to evaluate
